newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bundesbank says dollar recovery at an end.
newsitem.headline: Bundesbank says dollar recovery at an end.

text.p: The Bundesbank made clear on Thursday that it believed a recovery in the dollar from an all-time low in 1995 had come to an end, and expressed concern about a surge in the German stock market.

"We are now in a phase in which the correction has clearly come to an end," Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer told a news conference after the central bank's council met in the Bavarian town of Aschau,

He warned financial markets that the Bundesbank was now watching developments closely. The central bank was also determined that the mark would remain strong until it is exchanged for the planned single European currency.
"We will naturally watch the developments in markets. You can be sure that it is important for us that the mark remains a strong currency and enters the euro as a strong currency," Tietmeyer said.
The euro is scheduled for launching in 1999.
The mark has depreciated sharply against the dollar this year and was trading at 1.7620 to the dollar just before the start of the Bundesbank's news conference.
But after Tietmeyer's comments, the mark recovered significantly, standing at 1.7548 to the dollar at 1200 GMT.
Bundesbank council member Franz-Christoph Zeitler reinforced Tietmeyer's comments in remarks made to reporters after the news conference.

Zeitler said that the meeting of the Group of Seven industrial nations at the end of April had determined that the state of correction in the dollar/mark exchange rates had "more or less" come to an end.
"On the other hand, what we do not want is a push in the other direction," he said.

The central bank hinted at some concerns about asset price inflation, even though Tietmeyer told the news conference that inflation essentially remained under control and there appeared little danger of a price jump.

But in response to concerns about a leap of over 30 percent in German share prices this year and the possibility that this could lead to asset-driven inflation, the central bank said it would be looking closely at the market's gains.
The 30-share DAX index, in a downward correction from repeated surges to new highs this week, ended Thursday's bourse trade down 63.48 points at 3,992.38. Its record high was 4,066.09.

Bundesbank deputy president Johann Wilhelm Gaddum said the DAX gains would be discussed at a review of developments in M3 money supply, due to take place in two weeks' time. The central bank uses M3 as a key early inflation indicator when setting monetary policy.
Market developments would be a topic in that debate, he said, and the sharp rise in Germany's DAX share index in the first half of 1997 would receive special attention.
Tietmeyer later said he did not expect the central bank to change its target corridor for M3 money supply developments in the course of that debate.
"I see no reason at the moment for a change in the M3 money supply target," Tietmeyer told reporters.

The Bundesbank's 1997 target range is 3.5 to 6.5 percent. M3 money supply grew in May at an annualised rate of 7.0 percent from the final quarter of 1996, just above the target. In April, M3 grew 6.7 percent.
The central bank left its interest rates unchanged at the meeting in line with economists' expectations.
The discount rate remains at 2.50 percent and the Lombard rate at 4.50 percent.
